Tax law is not general; it is complex and full of exceptions. On top of that, it is constantly changing, and you can’t afford to rely on surface-level information.


TaxGPT is different from ChatGPT. It is built from the ground up specifically for tax. The training data along with how it interprets questions, all of that was designed specifically for tax professionals. It understands and interprets federal, state, and territory-level tax laws well. Whether you are[researching a corporate deduction rule or navigating multistate nexus thresholds](https://www.taxgpt.com/taxgpt-insights/tax-research-challenges) , TaxGPT gives you tailored and relevant guidance.


With ChatGPT, you often have to reframe your questions for context, double-check facts, and cross-reference everything manually to verify accuracy. With TaxGPT, one question returns a detailed, accurate response with IRS sources.

### Knowledge Cutoff and Outdated Information


One of the biggest risks of using ChatGPT for tax work isn't that it's frozen in time; it's that being current and being authoritative are two different things. Even with web browsing available on paid plans, ChatGPT is still pulling from whatever it finds on the open web. It's not grounded in primary tax authority, so what it hands back can be a blog post's interpretation of a rule, a forum thread, or in some cases, a citation that sounds official but doesn't actually exist.


And in tax, that's not a small problem. A confident answer built on a non-authoritative source, or a fabricated one, can shift the advice you give just as easily as outdated information can.


TaxGPT is different. It's built to work from verified, primary tax sources (IRS guidance, code sections, state authorities), not a general web crawl. Whether it's a new IRS notice, a state-level change, or an update to depreciation rules, you get an answer with a source you can actually click and verify.


Take R&D credit eligibility. Ask ChatGPT and you may get criteria that look reasonable but don't hold up when checked against the actual rule. Ask TaxGPT and you get the current rules with source links you can click and review yourself. That kind of traceability is what saves hours of second-guessing, instead of adding to them.


This is tax. You can't afford to work with unverified information. Switch to[TaxGPT](https://www.taxgpt.com/) and get answers grounded in primary sources you can trust.
